questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of an Inverse Function Using a Table
questions.problem:
The following table gives the values of functions $g(x)$ and ${g}^{′}(x)$ at some points. Find $({g}^{-1})^{′}(7).$

| **$x$** | $g(x)$ | ${g}^{′}(x)$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $-6$ | $9$ | $-1$ |
| $4$ | $7$ | $-4$ |
questions.worked_solution:
The formula for the derivative of the inverse is

$$
({g}^{-1})^{′}(x)=\frac{1}{{g}^{′}({g}^{-1}(x))}.
$$

Substituting $x=7,$ we have

$$
({g}^{-1})^{′}(7)=\frac{1}{{g}^{′}({g}^{-1}(7))}.
$$

From the table, we obtain ${g}^{-1}(7)=4$ and ${g}^{′}(4)=-4.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}({g}^{-1})^{′}(7) & =\frac{1}{{g}^{′}({g}^{-1}(7))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{g}^{′}(4)} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-4)} \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Derivative Using Properties of Inverse Functions
questions.problem: Consider the function $f(x)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-4).$ Given that $y=f(x)$ is invertible throughout its domain, determine $({f}^{-1})^{′}(0).$
questions.worked_solution:
To determine $({f}^{-1})^{′}(0),$ we use the following formula:

$$
{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(0)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(0))}
$$

First, we calculate the value of ${f}^{-1}(0).$ To do this, we solve the equation ${f}^{-1}(0)=x.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-1}(0) & =x \\ f(x) & =0 \\ x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-4) & =0 \\ x & =0,\,5.\end{aligned}
$$

We discard $x=0$ since the logarithm is not defined here. Therefore, ${f}^{-1}(0)=5.$

Now, we calculate ${f}^{′}(5),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-4) \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-4)+\frac{x}{x-4} \\ {f}^{′}(5) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(5-4)+\frac{5}{5-4} \\ {f}^{′}(5) & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(0) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(0))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(5)} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the function $f(x)=-3+5{e}^{x+1}.$ Given that $y=f(x)$ is invertible throughout its domain, determine $({f}^{-1})^{′}(2).$
questions.worked_solution:
To determine $({f}^{-1})^{′}(2),$ we use the following formula:

$$
{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(2)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(2))}
$$

First, we calculate the value of ${f}^{-1}(2).$ To do this, we solve the equation ${f}^{-1}(2)=x.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-1}(2) & =x \\ f(x) & =2 \\ -3+5{e}^{x+1} & =2 \\ 5{e}^{x+1} & =5 \\ {e}^{x+1} & =1 \\ x+1 & =0 \\ x & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${f}^{-1}(2)=-1.$

Now, we calculate ${f}^{′}(-1),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =-3+5{e}^{x+1} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =5{e}^{x+1} \\ {f}^{′}(-1) & =5{e}^{0} \\ {f}^{′}(-1) & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(2) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(2))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(-1)} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of an Inverse Function
questions.problem: Consider the function $f(x)=\frac{3x-2}{x+2}$ and the point $P(-1,-5)$ that lies on $y=f(x).$ Given that $f(x)$ is invertible in the vicinity of $P,$ the slope of $y={f}^{-1}(x)$ at the point $(-5,-1)$ is{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
We start by calculating the derivative of $f$ at the point $(-1,-5).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{3x-2}{x+2} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{8}{(x+2)^{2}} \\ {f}^{′}(-1) & =8\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $(-1,-5)$ lies on $y=f(x),$ we know that the corresponding point $(-5,-1)$ lies on $y={f}^{-1}(x).$

Furthermore, the slopes of the tangents to the two respective points are reciprocals. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}({f}^{-1})^{′}(-5) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(-5))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(-1)} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$
